answer.rationale: The dominant constraint is the primary objective's second clause: do not lose customer writes. memory_b2 explicitly rules out regional_failover here — it restored latency fast but opened a 40-minute replication gap and lost writes, with the standing instruction never to fail over while writes are hot. Settlement traffic is at daily peak and writes are heavy, so failover is disqualified regardless of how attractive its latency recovery looks. route_read_replicas (memory_b5) addressed read load stealing primary capacity from writes; nothing here indicates a dashboard/report read surge, so it is a plausible but unmatched analogy. add_capacity (memory_b3) worked for a pre-announced retail peak provisioned ahead of time; provisioning headroom reactively 90 minutes into a climb is slow and does not address a code-introduced regression. enable_circuit_breaker (memory_b4) contained an external partner outage; there is no partner failure signal here, and failing fast on the write path during settlement is exactly how writes get dropped. That leaves rollback_release, which is also the best causal match: a release went out 2 hours ago and latency began climbing 90 minutes ago, a 30-minute lag consistent with gradual rollout or connection-pool/warm-cache effects. I want the two rollback-relevant records verified because the summaries may be flattering. memory_b1 needs its original record because 'no customer impact' was recorded on a day-18 incident whose write volume was almost certainly nothing like settlement peak — I need to know whether that rollback ran against hot writes and whether the prior build was schema-compatible, since a backward-incompatible migration is the one way rollback itself destroys writes. memory_b6 needs verification because it cuts against my hypothesis: if staged gating reliably catches regressions within an hour in canary, this build already passed that gate, which weakens the release-caused theory and raises the chance the real driver is settlement peak load colliding with something else. If b6's original record shows gating coverage does not extend to write-path or settlement-shaped traffic, the release hypothesis strengthens considerably. Because two of the three current conditions (peak writes, release) each independently explain rising write latency, and I cannot distinguish them with one shot, I am scoping this as a small guarded test: roll back on a limited slice of write traffic and watch p99 on the rolled-back cohort against the control. If latency separates, the release is confirmed and I complete the rollback in the next window with full confidence; if both cohorts stay elevated, the cause is load and I have spent little and lost no writes. I am explicitly flagging downstream value risk: a rollback across a schema or message-format boundary can strand or corrupt in-flight settlement writes, so the guarded slice must be verified schema-compatible before it expands, and a fast abort path back to the current build must be ready. Confidence is moderate, not high — the timing correlation is suggestive but not causal proof, and memory_b6 is genuine evidence against it.
